nameStory: Slender leafy spurge gets its name from its narrow, leafy stems that distinguish it from other spurges. The word 'spurge' comes from the Old French 'espurgier,' meaning 'to purge,' referring to the plant's historical use as a harsh laxative. The milky sap was also called 'wolf's milk' in Europe, perhaps because it was considered as dangerous as nursing from a wolf!
description: Slender leafy spurge is a tall, upright perennial herb that can grow 2-4 feet high. It has narrow, blue-green leaves arranged alternately along smooth stems that branch near the top. The small yellowish-green flowers lack true petals and are surrounded by bright yellow-green bracts that look like tiny flowers. Like all spurges, it produces a distinctive milky white sap when broken.

idTips.label: Milky Sap
idTips.description: Break a stem or leaf and watch for the immediate appearance of thick, white, latex-like sap that looks like milk - this is the signature of all spurges and can cause skin irritation

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish-green flowers without petals, surrounded by bright yellow-green leaf-like bracts that form small cup-shaped clusters at branch tips in late spring to summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves about 1-3 inches long, arranged alternately up the stem, with a smooth texture and blue-green color that feels slightly waxy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect stems that branch primarily in the upper portion, forming an inverted triangle shape, with multiple stems often growing from the same root system

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small three-chambered capsules that split open explosively when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away with an audible pop

habitat: Found along roadsides, disturbed soils, field edges, and waste areas throughout New England, particularly in sunny locations with well-drained soil. As an invasive species from Europe and Asia, it often establishes in areas where native vegetation has been disturbed. It thrives in both sandy and clay soils and can tolerate drought conditions once established.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge early, showing the characteristic narrow blue-green leaves. Plants begin their rapid upward growth as soil warms.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from June through August, with the bright yellow-green bracts most visible. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive flower clusters are prominent.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and explosively disperse in late summer and early fall. Leaves may turn yellowish before the plant dies back to its root system.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely above ground, surviving as roots and underground stems that will produce new shoots in spring.

funFact: Slender leafy spurge has one of nature's most dramatic seed dispersal methods - its seed pods explode with enough force to launch seeds up to 15 feet away, and you can actually hear them popping on quiet summer days!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relative leafy spurge (Euphorbia esula), but slender leafy spurge has narrower leaves and a more slender overall appearance. Remember: if the leaves look like grass blades, think 'slender' spurge.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'leafy spurge' like its relative, this species is specifically the 'slender' leafy spurge - the naming can be confusing since both are leafy! This is an invasive species that's considered a serious agricultural pest in some areas, so land managers work actively to control its spread.
compareHints: Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves. Cypress spurge has much more needle-like leaves, while spotted spurge stays low to the ground. Flowering spurge has broader leaves and more showy white flower clusters, making slender leafy spurge the tall, narrow, yellow-green one of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
